prompt: Interior photograph of Tadao Ando's Church of the Light, 1989, Ibaraki, Japan: a small rectangular chapel of smooth grey cast-in-place concrete with visible circular formwork tie holes and crisp panel joints. The flat rear wall behind the altar is split by a cruciform slit of blinding white daylight: the vertical slit runs the FULL height of the wall from the floor to the ceiling, and the horizontal slit runs the FULL width of the wall, touching both side walls, so the glowing cross bleeds off all four edges of the rear wall like the wall has been cut into four quadrants. This cross is the ONLY light source in the room — absolutely no other windows, no skylights, no glowing gap or light seam where the ceiling meets the walls, every other surface in deep shadow lit only by spill from the cross. Rows of dark, rough scaffolding-plank pews flank a central aisle, and the dark floor steps gently down toward the simple wooden altar. Camera at seated eye level in the rear center of the aisle, perfectly symmetrical one-point perspective, high contrast, slight light bloom around the cross, photorealistic architectural photography, full-frame camera, 35mm lens, no people, no text anywhere in the image, no watermarks.

Architectural photograph of the Seagram Building, New York, 1958, by Ludwig Mies van der Rohe: a single slender 38-story bronze-and-grey-glass International Style tower, dramatically taller than it is wide, its FULL height visible in frame from plaza to roof parapet against a deep blue dusk sky. The curtain wall is a strict, unbroken grid of crisp vertical bronze I-beam mullions catching warm light, with interior office lights glowing in a perfectly uniform amber grid on every floor, identical rhythm from bottom to top. The tower stands set back on a wide, completely empty pink-granite pedestrian plaza raised above Park Avenue, with a long shallow reflecting pool in the foreground mirroring the lit facade; the base is recessed behind tall bronze pilotis with a glowing glass lobby. Camera at standing height at the plaza edge, vertical-format low three-quarter perspective looking up so the vertical mullion rhythm dominates and the slab's tall slender proportion is unmistakable. Period-correct 1958 details, photorealistic large-format architectural photography, Ezra Stoller style. The tower must clearly read as about 38 floors and several times taller than its width — do not render a short or squat building. The plaza is pedestrian-only: absolutely no cars, no roadway, and no parked vehicles anywhere on or beside the plaza or pool. No people in the foreground, no signage, no text anywhere in the image, no watermarks.

Subtle color-film grain, no text anywhere in the image, no watermarks.

Photorealistic 1970 motorsport photograph of a Porsche 917K short-tail (Kurzheck) endurance racing prototype in plain Gulf colors: the entire body light powder blue with ONE continuous marigold-orange center stripe running unbroken from the tip of the nose, up the front hood, over the windscreen header and roof, and down the rear deck to the very tail — the stripe must never stop at the windscreen and must be visibly continuous over the whole length of the car. Empty pit lane at golden hour, warm low sun, long shadows, fine film grain like a 1970 Le Mans documentary still, no text anywhere in the image, no watermarks.

Photorealistic luxury-craftsmanship photograph inside a leather atelier: a partially assembled structured handbag body in gold-tan full-grain calf leather — unmistakably a trapezoidal handbag in progress with side gussets and a fold-over front flap, wider at the base than the top, never a flat wallet or folio — held upright between the long wooden jaws of a traditional saddler's stitching clam gripped between the artisan's knees. Gallery installation photograph of Donald Judd's 1967 'Untitled (Stack)': a single vertical column of EXACTLY TWELVE identical closed rectangular boxes cantilevered from a tall flat white museum wall — count them, twelve units, no more, no fewer. Each box is a fully sealed shallow rectangular volume of galvanized iron with a glossy deep emerald-green lacquered front and sides and a flat closed metal top — none of the boxes is an open tray and no interiors are visible. Camera at the vertical midpoint of the column, straight-on view turned about 20 degrees to one side so box undersides are visible above the lens height and box tops below it, consistent single-point perspective. Soft even diffuse museum lighting, subtle reflections in the green lacquer and the polished concrete floor, photorealistic, no people, no text anywhere in the image, no watermarks

Every visible stitch must be a simple straight tack of thread: strictly no L-shaped marks, no corner brackets, no crop-mark or registration-mark shapes, no staples, no printed symbols, and no printing of any kind on the label or fabric.
